# Why this run exists

`fertility.qmd` asked what the tokenizer alone can account for, and found the
channel real but small. It could not say how far apart the aggregation
conventions actually are, because it never ran a model. This run does, at window
8 only, on a stratified subsample of both corpora.

Four policies, scored on the same words in the same pass so every comparison is
paired:

| Policy | Causal | Masked |
|---|---|---|
| `first` | the word's first subword, left context only. **The current convention.** | first subword with the whole word masked |
| `joint` | `-log P(word \| context)` by the chain rule. Exact. | within-word autoregressive scoring (Kauf & Ivanova 2023) |
| `density` | joint / *k*, per-subword information | joint / *k*, per-subword information |
| `joint_indep` | — | sum of the all-masked marginals, ignoring within-word dependence |

The question this has to answer is narrow and practical. Not whether `first` is
the theoretically preferred quantity, which it is not, but whether the chapter's
conclusions depend on it. Those conclusions are a validity ordering across
models, a fairness reading, and a selected configuration.

**Subsample, and what that does to the numbers.** 1,500 ELLIPSE essays
stratified on the holistic score, and 200 per L1 on TOEFL 11 stratified on level
within L1. Absolute `|r|` and `max |d|` therefore differ a little from the
full-corpus values in `pareto-analysis.qmd`. The decision-relevant quantity here
is the *difference between policies on identical essays*, which is paired and far
more precise than the subsample size suggests marginally.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

set.seed(42)
N_BOOT <- 2000
D_FLAG <- 0.10
LEVELS_ORD <- c("low", "medium", "high")
POLICY_LEVELS <- c("first", "joint", "density", "joint_indep")
POLICY_LABELS <- c(first = "first subword", joint = "joint",
                   density = "density", joint_indep = "joint (independent)")

find_results <- function() {
  d <- normalizePath(getwd())
  for (i in 1:6) {
    cand <- file.path(d, "results", "predictability")
    if (dir.exists(cand)) return(cand)
    d <- dirname(d)
  }
  stop("results/predictability not found")
}
RESULTS <- find_results()
for (hp in c("../_viz_helpers.R", "src/1-predictability-benchmark/_viz_helpers.R")) {
  if (file.exists(hp)) { source(hp); break }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: load
pol <- read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "subword_policy_long.csv.gz"),
                col_types = cols(text_id = col_character(), l1 = col_character(),
                                 level = col_character(), .default = col_guess())) |>
  mutate(policy = factor(policy, levels = POLICY_LEVELS),
         family = factor(model_family(model), levels = FAMILY_LEVELS))

MODELS <- sort(unique(pol$model))
ARCH <- pol |> distinct(model, arch) |> deframe()

ell <- filter(pol, corpus == "ellipse")
toe <- filter(pol, corpus == "toefl11") |>
  mutate(level = factor(level, levels = LEVELS_ORD))

cat(sprintf("%d models, %d ELLIPSE essays, %d TOEFL essays\n",
            length(MODELS), n_distinct(ell$text_id), n_distinct(toe$text_id)))
```

# Section 1 — Does this reproduce the production pipeline?

Before anything is read off this run, the re-implementation has to agree with the
one that produced the chapter. The production path scores a word by its first
subword under both architectures, so the `first` column should reproduce
`mean_surprisal_bits` at window 8. Spans are rebuilt from the offset mapping here
rather than reused from `get_token_alignment`, so a handful of words differ per
essay and exact equality is not expected; a high correlation and a small mean
offset are.

```{r}
#| label: verify
prod <- bind_rows(
  read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "ellipse_long.csv.gz"),
           col_types = cols(window = col_character(), text_id = col_character())) |>
    filter(window == "8") |> transmute(corpus = "ellipse", text_id, model,
                                       prod_bits = mean_surprisal_bits),
  read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "toefl_long.csv.gz"),
           col_types = cols(window = col_character(), text_id = col_character())) |>
    filter(window == "8") |> transmute(corpus = "toefl11", text_id, model,
                                       prod_bits = mean_surprisal_bits))

verify <- pol |>
  filter(policy == "first") |>
  inner_join(prod, by = c("corpus", "text_id", "model")) |>
  group_by(model, arch) |>
  summarise(r = cor(bits, prod_bits),
            mean_diff = mean(bits - prod_bits),
            max_abs_diff = max(abs(bits - prod_bits)),
            n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(r)

verify |>
  mutate(across(c(r, mean_diff, max_abs_diff), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Arch", "r with production", "Mean difference (bits)",
                      "Max |difference|", "n essays"))
```

`r if (min(verify$r) > 0.99) "Every model reproduces at r > .99, so the rest of this report is reading the same instrument the chapter reports." else "**A model falls below r = .99 against production. Investigate before reading on.**"`
The residual offset is the span rebuild plus bf16 arithmetic, and it is common to
all four policies, so it cancels in every paired comparison below.

# Section 2 — How far apart are the policies?

```{r}
#| label: divergence
div <- pol |>
  select(corpus, text_id, model, arch, policy, bits) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = bits)

div |>
  group_by(model, arch) |>
  summarise(first = mean(first), joint = mean(joint), density = mean(density),
            joint_over_first = mean(joint) / mean(first),
            r_first_joint = cor(first, joint),
            r_first_density = cor(first, density), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(arch, desc(joint_over_first)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Arch", "first", "joint", "density",
                      "joint / first", "r(first, joint)", "r(first, density)"))
```

The joint charges more than the first subword does, by construction, since it
adds the continuation pieces. What matters is that the two order essays almost
identically: `r(first, joint)` is what carries the validity through.

```{r}
#| label: split-words
pol |>
  filter(!is.na(bits_split), policy %in% c("first", "joint")) |>
  select(corpus, text_id, model, arch, policy, bits_split) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = bits_split) |>
  group_by(model, arch) |>
  summarise(first_split = mean(first), joint_split = mean(joint),
            ratio = mean(joint) / mean(first), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(ratio)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Arch", "first (split words)", "joint (split words)",
                      "joint / first"),
        caption = "Restricted to words the tokenizer split into two or more pieces.")
```

This is the number `fertility.qmd` could not produce. On the two-to-four per cent
of words that split, the joint charges roughly twice what the first subword does.
The convention is not a rounding error on those words. It survives to the essay
level only because those words are rare.

## A worked example

The corpus averages hide a distinction that decides how worried to be. One
sentence, scored by `policy_example.py` under the selected model and one masked
model, in bits.

```{r}
#| label: example
read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "subword_policy_example.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(k > 1 | word %in% c("rules", "every")) |>
  mutate(across(c(first, joint, density, joint_indep), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  select(model, word, k, pieces, first, joint, density, joint_indep) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Word", "k", "Subwords", "first", "joint",
                      "density", "joint (indep.)"),
        caption = "Split words, plus two unsplit words for reference.")
```

Two split words, opposite behaviour, and the difference is the whole argument.

*unpredictability* is a real English word. OLMo-2 cuts it `unpredict|ability`,
and having seen `unpredict` the continuation is nearly free, so `first` (21.85)
and `joint` (22.19) agree to within a third of a bit. The first subword already
carries essentially all of the word's information, which is exactly the case the
convention was implicitly assuming.

*misstake* is a misspelling. It is cut `mis|st|ake`, and the continuation is not
free at all, because nothing about `mis` predicts `st|ake`. `first` charges
14.62 bits and `joint` charges 26.57. Here the convention undercharges by nearly
half.

That is the mechanism behind everything in `fertility.qmd`. The words where
`first` and `joint` diverge are disproportionately the non-standard ones, and
non-standard forms are more frequent in lower-proficiency writing. Whether the
divergence is large enough at essay level to move a conclusion is what the rest
of this report measures.

The other two columns show why neither alternative is attractive. `density`
charges *less* for *misstake* than `first` does (19.69 against 18.29 for BERT,
and 8.86 against 14.62 for OLMo-2's three-piece cut), because dividing by *k*
rewards a word for having been cut up, which is the opposite of what a
proficiency measure wants. And `joint (indep.)` charges 74.79 bits for
*unpredictability* against the chain version's 44.89, which is why a masked joint
cannot be assembled from an all-masked pass and needs the extra forward passes
this run made.

# Section 3 — Validity

```{r}
#| label: validity
val <- ell |>
  group_by(model, arch, family, policy) |>
  summarise(abs_r = abs(cor(bits, overall)), .groups = "drop")

val |>
  select(model, arch, policy, abs_r) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = abs_r) |>
  arrange(desc(first)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  kable(caption = "ELLIPSE validity |r| by policy. Subsample; compare columns, not levels.")
```

```{r}
#| label: validity-boot
# Paired essay-level bootstrap on the change in |r| from `first` to `joint`.
wide_e <- ell |>
  filter(policy %in% c("first", "joint")) |>
  select(text_id, model, policy, bits, overall) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = bits) |>
  arrange(model, text_id)
ids_e <- unique(wide_e$text_id)
mods <- unique(wide_e$model)
Mf <- matrix(wide_e$first, nrow = length(ids_e), dimnames = list(NULL, mods))
Mj <- matrix(wide_e$joint, nrow = length(ids_e), dimnames = list(NULL, mods))
ye <- wide_e$overall[wide_e$model == mods[1]]

bd <- replicate(N_BOOT, {
  i <- sample.int(length(ids_e), replace = TRUE); yb <- ye[i]
  as.vector(abs(cor(Mj[i, ], yb))) - as.vector(abs(cor(Mf[i, ], yb)))
})
rownames(bd) <- mods

val_delta <- tibble(
  model = mods,
  d_abs_r = as.vector(abs(cor(Mj, ye))) - as.vector(abs(cor(Mf, ye))),
  lo = apply(bd, 1, quantile, 0.025),
  hi = apply(bd, 1, quantile, 0.975)) |>
  mutate(crosses_zero = lo <= 0 & hi >= 0) |>
  arrange(d_abs_r)

val_delta |>
  mutate(across(c(d_abs_r, lo, hi), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Δ|r| (joint − first)", "2.5%", "97.5%", "CI covers 0"),
        caption = paste0("Paired essay-level bootstrap, ", N_BOOT, " resamples."))
```

# Section 4 — Fairness

The same max `|d|` the main analysis uses: Cohen's *d* between each L1 group and
the rest within each proficiency stratum, standardized by the pooled
within-stratum SD, combined as a focal-group-size weighted average, then the
worst group.

```{r}
#| label: fairness
group_d <- function(y, l1, level, strata = LEVELS_ORD) {
  groups <- sort(unique(l1))
  vapply(groups, function(g) {
    num <- 0; wsum <- 0
    for (s in strata) {
      in_s <- level == s
      a <- y[in_s & l1 == g]; b <- y[in_s & l1 != g]
      n1 <- length(a); n2 <- length(b)
      if (n1 < 2L || n2 < 2L) next
      sp <- sqrt(((n1 - 1) * var(a) + (n2 - 1) * var(b)) / (n1 + n2 - 2))
      num <- num + n1 * (mean(a) - mean(b)) / sp; wsum <- wsum + n1
    }
    num / wsum
  }, numeric(1))
}

fair <- toe |>
  group_by(model, arch, policy) |>
  group_modify(\(d, k) {
    dd <- group_d(d$bits, d$l1, as.character(d$level))
    tibble(max_abs_d = max(abs(dd)), worst_l1 = names(dd)[which.max(abs(dd))],
           n_flag = sum(abs(dd) >= D_FLAG))
  }) |>
  ungroup()

fair |>
  select(model, arch, policy, max_abs_d) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = max_abs_d) |>
  arrange(first) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  kable(caption = "TOEFL 11 max |d| by policy. Lower is fairer.")

fair |>
  filter(policy %in% c("first", "joint")) |>
  select(model, arch, policy, worst_l1, n_flag) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = c(worst_l1, n_flag)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Arch", "Worst L1 (first)", "Worst L1 (joint)",
                      "Groups flagged (first)", "Groups flagged (joint)"))
```

# Section 5 — Does the selection change?

This is the only question with a consequence for the chapter. The rule is: take
the highest-validity configuration class, then within it the smallest model with
a publicly released pretraining corpus. At window 8 the class is the generative
models, and the pick is `olmo2-1b`.

```{r}
#| label: selection
rank_tbl <- val |>
  filter(policy %in% c("first", "joint", "density")) |>
  select(model, arch, policy, abs_r) |>
  group_by(policy) |>
  mutate(rank = rank(-abs_r)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(model, arch, policy, rank) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = rank) |>
  arrange(first)

rank_tbl |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Arch", "Rank under first", "Rank under joint",
                      "Rank under density"),
        caption = "Validity rank, 1 = highest |r|.")

class_tbl <- val |>
  filter(policy %in% c("first", "joint")) |>
  group_by(policy, arch) |>
  summarise(mean_abs_r = mean(abs_r), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = mean_abs_r)

class_tbl |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Architecture class", "Mean |r| (first)", "Mean |r| (joint)"),
        caption = "The class comparison the selection rule reads.")
```

```{r}
#| label: selection-readout
spearman <- cor(rank_tbl$first, rank_tbl$joint, method = "spearman")
top_first <- rank_tbl$model[which.min(rank_tbl$first)]
top_joint <- rank_tbl$model[which.min(rank_tbl$joint)]
causal_wins_first <- class_tbl$first[class_tbl$arch == "causal"] >
                     class_tbl$first[class_tbl$arch == "masked"]
causal_wins_joint <- class_tbl$joint[class_tbl$arch == "causal"] >
                     class_tbl$joint[class_tbl$arch == "masked"]
cat(sprintf("Rank correlation first vs joint: %.3f\n", spearman))
cat(sprintf("Highest |r|: %s under first, %s under joint\n", top_first, top_joint))
cat(sprintf("Causal class beats masked class: %s under first, %s under joint\n",
            causal_wins_first, causal_wins_joint))
cat(sprintf("Models changing rank: %d of %d; largest move %d place(s)\n",
            sum(rank_tbl$first != rank_tbl$joint), nrow(rank_tbl),
            max(abs(rank_tbl$first - rank_tbl$joint))))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-policy
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
plot_df <- val |>
  filter(policy %in% c("first", "joint", "density")) |>
  left_join(fair |> select(model, policy, max_abs_d), by = c("model", "policy"))

p_pol <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(max_abs_d, abs_r, colour = family, shape = policy)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = model), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = FAMILY_COLORS, drop = TRUE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(first = 16, joint = 17, density = 1),
                     labels = unname(POLICY_LABELS[c("first", "joint", "density")])) +
  labs(x = "TOEFL 11 max |d|  (lower is fairer)", y = "ELLIPSE validity  |r|",
       colour = "Family", shape = "Policy",
       title = "Each model under three aggregation policies",
       subtitle = "Grey lines join the same model. Window 8, subsample.") +
  theme_study1(base_size = 11)
p_pol
save_fig(p_pol, "subword_policy_plane", width = 8, height = 5)
```

# Section 6 — The masked arm

Masked models admit one policy the causal models do not, since a masked LM has
no chain rule to appeal to, and they are also where the four policies spread
furthest apart. All four are reported here.

```{r}
#| label: masked
#| eval: !expr any(pol$arch == "masked")
masked_tbl <- val |>
  filter(arch == "masked") |>
  select(model, policy, abs_r) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = abs_r) |>
  left_join(fair |> filter(arch == "masked") |>
              select(model, policy, max_abs_d) |>
              pivot_wider(names_from = policy, values_from = max_abs_d,
                          names_prefix = "d_"), by = "model")

masked_tbl |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  kable(caption = "Masked models only. |r| columns first, then max |d| columns.")

div |>
  filter(arch == "masked") |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(joint = mean(joint), joint_indep = mean(joint_indep),
            overcharge = mean(joint_indep) - mean(joint),
            r = cor(joint, joint_indep), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "joint (chain)", "joint (independent)",
                      "Overcharge (bits)", "r"),
        caption = "What ignoring within-word dependence costs.")
```

The independent version charges more than the chain version, as it must: masking
every subword of a word at once throws away the fact that a word's pieces predict
each other. That is the reason a masked joint cannot be assembled from the
existing all-masked pass and needs the extra forward passes this run made.

# Read-out

```{r}
#| label: readout
sel_r <- val |> filter(model == "olmo2-1b") |> select(policy, abs_r) |> deframe()
sel_d <- fair |> filter(model == "olmo2-1b") |> select(policy, max_abs_d) |> deframe()
cat(sprintf("olmo2-1b/8   |r|: first %.3f, joint %.3f (Δ %+.3f)\n",
            sel_r["first"], sel_r["joint"], sel_r["joint"] - sel_r["first"]))
cat(sprintf("olmo2-1b/8 max|d|: first %.3f, joint %.3f (Δ %+.3f)\n",
            sel_d["first"], sel_d["joint"], sel_d["joint"] - sel_d["first"]))
cat(sprintf("Median |r(first, joint)| across models: %.4f\n",
            median(div |> group_by(model) |> summarise(r = cor(first, joint)) |> pull(r))))
```
